one_liner: Go LZ77 compressor (new byte-aligned format, Snappy/S2 successor) that compresses faster and smaller than LZ4's fastest mode.
what_it_does: MinLZ is a Go package and `mz` command-line tool implementing the MinLZ v1.0 format: a byte-oriented LZ77 block format (blocks up to 8 MB) plus a framed stream format of independent, checksummed blocks with EOF validation, optional seek index and optional Bloom-filter search chunks. The API mirrors klauspost/compress S2: `minlz.Encode(dst, src, level)` / `minlz.Decode(dst, src)` for blocks and `NewWriter`/`NewReader` (io.Writer/io.Reader, io.ReaderFrom/WriterTo, concurrent encode/decode) for streams. Four levels: SuperFast (-1), Fastest (1), Balanced (2), Smallest (3). Its decoders also read existing Snappy and S2 content, but MinLZ output cannot be read by Snappy, S2 or LZ4.
how_it_is_fast: The format has no entropy coding and no table-driven or context-dependent decoding: four tag types (literal/repeat, 10-bit, 16-bit and up-to-21-bit offset copies) with fused literal+copy forms, so a decoder is a branch-predictable byte loop. Copy2/Copy3 forbid offsets under 64 bytes so the decoder can always use 64-byte wide copies without overlap checks, and fused literals can be copied 4 bytes at a time unconditionally (SPEC.md 'Implementation Notes'). The Go package adds hand-written AMD64 and ARM64 encoder and decoder assembly, hash-table greedy matching at the fast levels, and streams of independent blocks compressed and decompressed on many goroutines (default GOMAXPROCS writers, up to 8 decoders).
when_to_use: Go services that compress on the hot path (RPC payloads, caches, object storage, logs) where Snappy or S2 is in use and you can change the wire format: same API shape, smaller output, and old Snappy/S2 data still decodes.

Multi-GB streams on many-core machines where compression throughput matters more than ratio: the README's 6.27 GB JSON stream shows MinLZ 1 at 14,921 MiB/s and 84.47% reduction vs LZ4 Fastest at 5,860 MiB/s and 79.69% (16-core Ryzen 9 3950X, package concurrency).
Seekable compressed streams: independent blocks plus an optional index allow random access and parallel decode without an external container.
Mostly-text or structured data (JSON, CSV, logs, protobuf) where an 'always on' compressor should run near memory bandwidth; it detects already-compressed data quickly and stores it.
when_not_to_use: C++ projects: the maintained implementation is Go (plus Rust ports); the only C port is an experimental, machine-converted CC0 gist (block format only, 'not production level code').
Decompression-bound workloads on small cached blocks: the README itself says 'LZ4 is decompression speed king' (protobuf block: LZ4 0 at 137,553 MB/s vs MinLZ 1 at 116,762 MB/s, 16 threads).
Interchange with tools that expect LZ4, Snappy or gzip: MinLZ is a new format with no external decoders beyond its own ports.

Archival or ratio-first storage: no entropy coding, so zstd gives smaller output; the spec itself points long-term storage to zstd. Level 3 also compresses slowly (210 MB/s on the protobuf block, 576 MiB/s on the JSON stream).
Raw blocks without your own checksum: the block API does no integrity check; only the stream format carries checksums and EOF markers.

integration.min_toolchain: Go 1.25 per go.mod; README promises support for the two Go releases before the current one
integration.platforms: any Go target (pure Go); assembly encoders and decoders on amd64 and arm64; build tags noasm, nounsafe, purego turn off assembly and/or unsafe
integration.thread_safety: Writers and Readers are per-stream objects (README recommends reusing them across streams); a stream encoder/decoder uses internal goroutines (WriterConcurrency, DecompressConcurrent). Block Encode/Decode are plain functions on caller buffers; concurrent use of one Writer is not documented.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — not for LZ4 (different format and language); near drop-in for Go Snappy/S2 users since decoders accept Snappy and S2 content and the API shape matches S2

gotchas: Output is not deterministic across builds: assembly and pure-Go encoders 'will often produce slightly different output' (README; issue #12 'Compression output dependent on architecture'), so do not hash compressed bytes for deduplication.
Block decode needs the exact compressed length; trailing bytes are an error, and blocks carry no checksum.

Recent fixed issues show the asm/pure-Go paths drift: #68 (closed 2026-09-28) amd64 encodeBlockFast returned buffers to the wrong sync.Pool, so LevelSuperFast reallocated tables every block (allocation cost only, output unaffected); #59 Balanced asm slower than pure Go on incompressible input; #63 pure-Go fast encoders stored a 10-byte repeating pattern uncompressed; #14 Snappy blocks over 8 MB failed to decode via the MinLZ block decoder.
README block numbers are 16-thread aggregates on cache-hot data; single-stream, single-core speeds are lower and the README explains streams are memory-bandwidth bound.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick MinLZ over LZ4 when you are in Go, control both ends of the format, and care about compression speed and ratio at the fastest level; keep LZ4 (or lzvolt/ZXC) when decode speed or a C/C++ library is the priority. Over klauspost/compress S2, pick it for a few percent smaller output and faster stream decode at similar compress speed (JSON stream: 3,204 vs 2,378 MiB/s decode).
verified_claims_summary: First-party README tables on an AMD Ryzen 9 3950X: on the Snappy-testdata protobuf block with 16 concurrent threads, MinLZ 1 compresses at 27,837 MB/s to 17,613 bytes vs LZ4 level 0 at 12,649 MB/s and 18,766 bytes, while LZ4 decodes faster (137,553 vs 116,762 MB/s); on a 6.27 GB JSON stream using each package's own concurrency, MinLZ 1 compresses at 14,921 MiB/s and decodes at 3,204 MiB/s vs LZ4 Fastest at 5,860 and 2,680 MiB/s. Go version, build flags and the LZ4 implementation/binding are not stated, and the identical 12,649 MB/s for LZ4 0 and LZ4 9 looks like a table copy error.
status_note: Actively maintained by MinIO (v1.2.0, issues fixed through late September 2026), Apache-2.0; usable directly from Go, while C++ users need cgo or the experimental CC0 C block port.
